steps.body: Pair objects one to one instead of judging the space they fill. An unmatched object identifies the larger group.
steps.narration: Pair objects one to one instead of judging the space they fill. An unmatched object identifies the larger group.

widget.prompt: Two groups look close. Build the count of the SPREAD-OUT group: it has 6.

commonCounts.feedback: The spreading fooled the eye upward; touching each one ends the count at six.
Undercounting the spread group misses one; every member gets a number.

widget.missFeedback: Count the spread group member by member; space between them adds nothing.
widget.successFeedback: Six — spread wide it looked like more, but the count ignores the spacing.

predict.prompt: A spread-out 6 against a squeezed 7 — which LOOKS bigger?
predict.reveal: Spacing inflates the look of a group, which is exactly why close calls need counting.

cml.actionGoal: Pair the groups one to one, or place both numbers in the counting song, for kcm compare visual.
invariants: Comparison rests on two facts that never move: pairing one to one leaves the bigger group with leftovers, and a number later in the counting song always names more — which is what kcm compare visual uses.
misconceptions: Judging by how much space a group fills, by the size of the things in it, or by which number was written first.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more joined the smaller group, would the pairing come out even?

widget.prompt: When is a quick visual estimate most reliable?

options.label: When one group uses larger objects
options.feedback: Object size can mislead; comparison is about how many objects there are.

options.label: When one group is clearly larger
options.feedback: Correct — an obvious gap can support a quick estimate, and pairing or counting can confirm it.

options.label: When one group is spread farther
options.feedback: Spacing can mislead; a spread-out group can contain fewer objects.

options.label: When the groups use different objects
options.feedback: Different kinds of objects can still be paired and counted fairly.

commonCounts.feedback: 5 matches the reference, so it is not more.

widget.prompt: There are 5 stars and 6 hearts. Which statement is true?

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Equal needs the pairing to come out even; here one side is left holding extras (5 against 6).

options.label: More stars
options.feedback: Pairing one to one uses every star with hearts to spare, so the stars are not the larger group.

options.label: More hearts
options.feedback: Correct — 6 hearts against 5 stars; pairing one to one leaves hearts unmatched.

options.label: You cannot tell
options.feedback: You can always tell — pair the groups one to one and look at which side has leftovers.

widget.prompt: Start at 13 and count on 4. Tap where you land.

commonLandings.feedback: 16 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 17.
18 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 4 hops from 13 to land on 17.

widget.missFeedback: Count 4 on from 13: you land on 17.
widget.successFeedback: 13 and 4 more is 17 — every step forward lands on a greater number.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — all 4 counts are needed to reach 17.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count-on stops after 4 numbers, on 17.

takeaways: A glance works for big gaps.

concept.body: The rule: trust a glance for big gaps, and reach for pairing or counting the moment the race looks close.
concept.narration: The rule: trust a glance for big gaps, and reach for pairing or counting the moment the race looks close.

widget.prompt: When can your eyes alone compare two groups safely?

options.label: When one group is clearly much bigger than the other
options.feedback: Correct — a big gap is visible at a glance; close contests need pairing or counting.

options.label: Always — eyes never fool us
options.feedback: Spread-out groups look bigger than they are; close comparisons fool the eye easily.

options.label: Never — you must always count
options.feedback: Seven against two needs no count; it is close contests that demand care.

options.label: Only when the groups are equal
options.feedback: Equal groups are exactly the hardest case for eyes alone — the pairing settles it.
